description: Flagship Sims: large, graphically ambitious simulations written for the strongest models (CLI agents). Each has numbered, checkable requirements and its own generation folder.

prompts.title: Airport Operations Simulator
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js airport operations simulator: a busy two-runway international airport seen from a free 3D camera, where the player is the duty manager balancing arrivals, departures, gates and ground crews through a whole day. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. A procedurally built airfield: two parallel runways with numbers, edge and centreline lights; a taxiway network with hold-short lines; a terminal with at least 10 gates and jet bridges; a control tower, apron stands and a cargo area.
2. Aircraft in at least 3 size classes (regional, narrow-body, wide-body) built from simple meshes with airline liveries, landing gear and blinking navigation and beacon lights. Wide-bodies only fit wide-body gates.
3. A data-driven schedule for one simulated day (06:00 to 24:00) of arrivals and departures with airline, class and time, shown on a split-flap style board that updates live: On time, Boarding, Delayed, Landed, Departed.
4. Aircraft follow real paths: final approach and flare, rollout and runway exit, taxi to the gate along the taxiway graph (shortest path, never across grass), pushback by a tug, taxi to the hold point, line-up and take-off roll with rotation.
5. Separation rules: one aircraft on a runway at a time, minimum spacing between landings, queues at hold-short lines, and taxiing aircraft stop behind each other instead of overlapping.
6. Each gate turnaround is a visible, timed sequence: the jet bridge docks, baggage carts and a belt loader arrive, a fuel truck connects, a catering truck lifts, then pushback. Every ground vehicle drives from its depot and back along service roads.
7. Passengers flow through a cut-away terminal (check-in, security queue, gate lounge, boarding), drawn as instanced figures whose queue lengths match the numbers in the HUD.
8. Weather and time of day: a full day and night cycle with sunrise and sunset light, runway and apron floodlights after dark, and weather events (fog cuts the landing rate, crosswind gusts cause go-arounds, a thunderstorm halts ground work) that cascade into delays.
9. Player decisions: drag an aircraft to reassign its gate, open extra security lanes at a staff cost, hold or expedite departures, and switch runway mode (mixed, or one runway for arrivals and one for departures).
10. A live KPI panel (on-time performance, average delay, movements per hour, gate use, passengers in the terminal) with a chart of delay across the day, and an end-of-day report with a grade.
11. Camera: free orbit and zoom, a follow-cam on a selected aircraft, and a tower-view preset. Clicking an aircraft shows its flight, state and turnaround timers.
12. A settings panel exposes the main variables (flights per hour, turnaround minutes per class, security throughput, weather frequency, seed) with reset to defaults. Pause and 1x/2x/5x/20x speed run on a fixed timestep, and the same seed replays the same day.

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: aircraft sliding sideways or teleporting between states; two aircraft on one runway; taxiing across grass instead of along the taxiway graph; ground vehicles appearing at a gate without driving there; a departures board that disagrees with what happens; weather that changes the look but not the throughput; speed changes altering outcomes.

prompts.title: Bus Garage Depot Simulator
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js bus garage simulator: a city bus depot through a full 24 hours, where the player runs the garage so every bus leaves on time for its route, fuelled, charged, clean and safe. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. A 3D depot: a covered parking hall with marked lanes where buses park nose to tail, so a bus can leave only when the ones in front have gone; a fuel island; electric charging bays; a drive-through wash with spinning brushes and water spray; a maintenance shed with inspection pits and lifts; a staff canteen; entry and exit gates.
2. A fleet of at least 40 buses of 3 types (single-deck diesel, double-deck hybrid, single-deck electric) in a fleet livery with fleet numbers, each tracking fuel or battery, mileage and defects.
3. A 24-hour timetable: the morning peak pull-out (about 05:00 to 07:30) sends most of the fleet out, buses come back between peaks and overnight. A dispatch board lists route, duty, driver and bus for every departure.
4. The lane-blocking puzzle: when a due bus is blocked in its lane, the sim shows it and either a shunter moves the buses in front (costing time) or the departure runs late. The player picks the parking rule for incoming buses: first free lane, by next departure time, or by bus type.
5. Every returning bus runs the servicing line in order (fuel or charge, wash, interior clean, park), each step with a visible queue and timer. Electric buses need a charger, and a site-wide power limit slows charging when many are plugged in.
6. Defects and maintenance: faults (tyres, brakes, doors, battery) arise with mileage and send a bus to the shed, where mechanics on shifts repair it on a lift or over a pit. Safety inspections fall due every N days.
7. Drivers and shifts: drivers sign on at the canteen, walk to their bus and run their duty. Late sign-ons, sickness and overtime are modelled, and no bus leaves without a driver.
8. Believable vehicle motion: buses follow drive paths with real turning circles (no turning on the spot), reverse into bays where needed, and never pass through each other or through walls.
9. Lighting: yard lights at night, headlights and brake lights, wet-ground reflections after the wash and in rain, and a day and night cycle seen through the open sides of the hall.
10. KPIs: lost mileage (missed or late departures), fleet availability, fuel and electricity used and their cost, shunting moves and the maintenance backlog, with a chart across the day and an end-of-day report.
11. Camera: orbit, plus a top-down plan view showing lane occupancy as a colour-coded grid. Clicking a bus shows its card: fleet number, type, fuel or charge, defects and next duty.
12. A settings panel exposes fleet mix, number of chargers and the power limit, wash and fuel throughput, fault rate, shunter count, parking rule and seed, with reset to defaults. Pause and 1x/2x/5x/20x speed run on a fixed timestep, deterministic for a seed.

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: buses driving through each other; lane blocking ignored (blocked buses leave anyway); servicing steps skipped; electric buses never held back by the power limit; buses turning on the spot; a dispatch board unrelated to what actually leaves.

prompts.title: Black Hole Expedition
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js black hole flight simulator: pilot a research ship on a decaying orbit around a supermassive black hole, collecting data from anomalies (gravitational-wave echoes, radiation bursts) before tidal forces tear the ship apart. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. Gravitational lensing as a full-screen shader: the background starfield, a distant galaxy and a faint space-time grid are bent around the black hole by stepping light rays through an approximate Schwarzschild deflection, producing an Einstein ring and a secondary image.
2. A volumetric accretion disk: hundreds of thousands of GPU particles (or a raymarched disk) on Keplerian orbits, inner edge faster, coloured by temperature from blue-white inside to deep orange outside, with Doppler beaming so the approaching side is brighter and bluer.
3. The far side of the disk is visibly lensed above and below the black hole's shadow, and the shadow and photon ring are sized correctly relative to the event horizon.
4. Relativistic jets: bright X-ray jets from both poles with animated turbulence.
5. HDR rendering with tone mapping, bloom and auto exposure that adapts between the pitch-black shadow and the blinding disk and jets.
6. A procedural research ship lit by the disk: its light colour and intensity follow how much of the disk is visible from the ship.
7. Flight on a pseudo-Newtonian potential so there is an innermost stable orbit: thrust, attitude control, and a predicted-orbit line. Dropping inside the innermost stable orbit spirals the ship in.
8. Gameplay: anomalies appear on set orbits; flying within range and holding a scan gathers data; tidal stress on the hull rises close to the hole; fuel is limited. Win by collecting the target data and escaping; lose by over-stressing the hull or crossing the horizon.
9. Time dilation: the HUD shows ship time against distant time, and near the hole the outside universe visibly speeds up (starfield twinkle, pulsar ticks).
10. Spaghettification near the end: the ship model stretches radially as it approaches the horizon.
11. HUD: distance in Schwarzschild radii, speed as a fraction of c, fuel, hull stress and data collected, plus a mini orbit diagram.
12. A settings panel exposes black hole mass (scaling the radius), disk density and brightness, lensing quality (ray steps), particle count, bloom and exposure, with reset to defaults, plus pause and a photo mode (free camera, HUD hidden).

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: 'lensing' that is a radial blur or distortion texture instead of bent rays; a disk with no Doppler asymmetry or no lensed far side; a flat textured ring instead of a volumetric disk; orbits that ignore gravity or are never stable; fixed exposure so the disk is blown out or the shadow is grey.

prompts.title: Microscopic Biosphere Defense
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js real-time strategy simulation set inside a drop of pond water or the bloodstream: the player commands immune cells and nano-drones defending a living ecosystem against invading bacteria and viruses. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. A 3D microscopic world: a fluid volume with organic terrain (membranes, cell walls), floating debris and drifting particles, all procedural.
2. Translucent organic materials with a subsurface-scattering approximation (wrap lighting plus thickness-based back-light transmission), so membranes glow when backlit and organelles show inside cells.
3. Microscope depth of field: a bokeh post-process with a focus distance the player controls, shallow enough that out-of-focus particles become soft bokeh discs.
4. Viscous fluid physics: low-Reynolds-number motion where drag dominates and nothing coasts, a flow field (curl noise or a small grid fluid solver) carrying debris and units, and wakes from moving units that push nearby debris.
5. At least 4 player unit types with distinct procedural shapes and animation (pseudopods, cilia, flagella): a macrophage that engulfs, a neutrophil that bursts in an area attack, a B-cell that marks enemies with antibodies, and a nano-drone that repairs tissue.
6. At least 3 enemy types: bacteria that divide over time, viruses that infect host cells and turn them into spawners, and a toxic biofilm that grows across surfaces.
7. RTS controls: box select, right-click move and attack, control groups, a minimap, and nutrients gathered from particles to produce units at a lymph-node structure.
8. Infection: host cells have health; infected cells change colour and pulse, then release virions after a timer; unchecked infection spreads exponentially. Win by keeping the infection cleared for a set time; lose if healthy host cells fall below a threshold.
9. Engulfing is animated: a macrophage deforms around its target (vertex shader) and visibly digests it.
10. Microscope looks: chromatic aberration and vignette, plus switchable stain modes (phase contrast, fluorescence false colour) that change the whole render.
11. HUD: nutrients, unit counts, infection percentage and wave timer, with tooltips on hover.
12. A settings panel exposes viscosity and flow strength, division rate, infection timer, depth-of-field strength, particle count and seed, with reset to defaults, pause and speed control.

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: units that glide like spaceships with no viscous drag; depth of field that is a uniform blur rather than depth-based; 'subsurface scattering' that is only transparency; bacteria that never divide; infection that does not spread; no box selection.

prompts.title: Neon Glassblowing Studio
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js crafting simulator: a calm, precise glassblowing session in a high-tech cyberpunk studio, shaping glowing glass sculptures filled with neon gas, metallic flakes and coloured canes. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. A detailed dark workshop: a glowing furnace (glory hole), workbench and tools, metal racks, a reflective floor and neon signage.
2. Shaping on a rotating blowpipe: the piece is a surface of revolution (a profile of about 64 points) that the player deforms live by blowing (inflate), pulling, pinching with jacks, flattening with a paddle and twisting (spiral ridges), by dragging along the profile and with tool keys.
3. Thermal state: every profile section has a temperature that falls over time and rises in the furnace. Hot glass glows with blackbody colour (white, yellow, orange, red) and is soft; cool glass is rigid and clear, so the player must reheat to keep working. The crossover from glowing to clear is visible.
4. Refraction: the glass bends the scene behind it (screen-space refraction from a background render target, offset by thickness and IOR), with Fresnel reflections of an environment map and chromatic dispersion at the edges.
5. Caustics: light through the glass casts animated caustic patterns on the bench, derived from the glass normals (light-space render or projected caustic texture).
6. Colour and inclusions: coloured frit, metallic flakes and twisted colour canes embed in the surface and follow its deformation. A neon gas fill (chosen colour) lights the hollow interior.
7. Emissive lighting: the neon fill and the hot glass light the room (dynamic coloured lights), with bloom and moody reflections.
8. Annealing: a finished piece goes into the annealer. Cooling it too fast in the open (a thermal-shock rule on the temperature gradient between sections) cracks it, with visible crack lines or a shatter.
9. A gallery: finished pieces stand on display shelves in the studio, kept in localStorage and re-rendered from their parameters, and each profile exports as JSON.
10. Procedural audio via Web Audio: furnace roar, a glass ring when tapped, a soft ambient pad, and a mute toggle.
11. Camera: orbit around the piece, a macro close-up preset, and a showroom turntable for finished pieces.
12. A settings panel exposes furnace temperature, cooling rate, IOR, dispersion, caustic intensity, bloom and neon colour, with reset to defaults and pause.

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: 'refraction' that is only opacity; hot and cold glass behaving the same; deformations that break rotational symmetry; caustics missing or static; inclusions that ignore deformation; neon light that does not reach the room.

prompts.title: Deep-Sea Vent Colony
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js deep-sea survival and colony-management simulator: a bioluminescent research base clinging to a volcanic trench miles below the surface, lit only by floodlights and living things. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. An abyssal trench: basalt pillow-lava terrain and black-smoker chimneys (procedural columns) pouring churning black smoke plumes.
2. Volumetric murk: depth fog with light scattering, so floodlights and creature lights cast visible cones and shafts (raymarched or layered volumes), and marine snow drifts and glints where it is lit.
3. Only artificial and biological light: no sunlight. The base floodlights can be toggled and aimed, and away from lights the scene is near black.
4. Bioluminescent life: an anglerfish with a lure, pulsing jellyfish with trailing verlet-rope tentacles, glowing coral and tube worms around the vents, and fish schools (boids) that avoid or seek light by species. Their light colours the rock around them.
5. Thermal plumes: hot water rising from vents distorts the view behind it (screen-space heat-haze refraction) and lifts particles; currents (a flow field) move snow, smoke and jellyfish.
6. Colony building: modules (habitat, thermal-vent generator, lab, chemosynthesis farm, docking bay) placed on the trench wall and joined by tunnels, each needing power, oxygen and pressure integrity.
7. Resources and needs: oxygen, power, food, hull integrity and crew morale. Vent output varies, and events (earthquake, eruption, hull breach, giant squid sighting) demand a response.
8. A submersible the player pilots in third person with its own lights, to collect samples, repair modules and scan species into a species log.
9. Pressure: a depth meter, creaking hull sounds, and visible damage (cracks, sparks, leaking bubbles).
10. Procedural audio via Web Audio: a low drone, sonar pings, creature calls and bubbles, with a mute toggle.
11. HUD and colony panel: resources with trends, module status, species discovered and crew.
12. A settings panel exposes fog density, marine snow count, plume strength, creature count, event frequency and light quality, with reset to defaults, pause and speed control.

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: a scene lit by ambient light instead of being near black; fog without light shafts; bioluminescence that lights nothing around it; no heat haze; colony numbers that ignore building; jellyfish as rigid meshes.

prompts.title: Architectural Demolition Sandbox
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js physics sandbox for demolishing or renovating buildings: a glass-and-steel tower, an ancient stone ruin and a brutalist concrete block, each brought down (or saved) piece by piece. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. Three buildings to choose from, each built procedurally from individual parts (blocks, floor slabs, columns, beams, glass panes): thousands of rigid bodies, not one mesh.
2. A rigid-body engine (cannon-es or Rapier from a CDN, or your own with a broadphase) running at least 5,000 active bodies interactively, with sleeping, rendered through InstancedMesh. Parts start joined by breakable bonds whose strength depends on material.
3. Structural integrity: load flows through the structure, removing a column overloads its neighbours, and supports failing in turn cause progressive collapse. A stress view colours elements by load from green to red.
4. Demolition tools on a budget: a wrecking ball swinging from a crane, explosive charges with a timed sequence editor for controlled implosions, a hydraulic breaker for single elements, and cutters for steel beams. Each costs money.
5. Fracture: glass panes shatter into shards, concrete splits into smaller chunks on hard impacts (pre-fractured or runtime Voronoi), and steel bends or drops whole.
6. Dust and debris: lit dust clouds billow from impacts and collapses, linger and settle, with small debris particles.
7. Procedural materials: concrete with aggregate and form-tie holes, veined marble, timber grain and reflective glass, with generated normal and roughness maps that hold up in close-up.
8. Dynamic lighting: a sun with shadows plus sky light and screen-space ambient occlusion. As floors fall, interiors open to the sky and become sunlit, with shadows updated every frame.
9. Renovation mode: reinforce instead of demolish (add steel braces, replace columns), then run an earthquake test to see whether it stands.
10. Scoring for controlled implosions (collapse within the footprint, spare the neighbouring building, stay under budget), with a slow-motion replay of the last collapse from several cameras.
11. Camera: orbit, first-person walk, slow motion and replay.
12. A settings panel exposes the building, material strengths, gravity, body count, dust amount and time scale, with reset to defaults and pause.

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: a building that is one mesh exploding into pre-baked pieces; no progressive collapse (removing a support does nothing); pieces jittering forever with no sleeping; unlit flat dust sprites; no replay; frame rate collapsing because every body is its own mesh.

prompts.title: Toy Brick Sandbox and Stop-Motion Studio
prompts.prompt:
Build a single-page Three.js building simulator with generic interlocking toy bricks: assemble models, stress-test them with physics, and animate them in a built-in stop-motion studio. Use no real toy brand names, logos or trademarked designs anywhere. This is a flagship brief: every numbered requirement must work and be visible on screen, not just described in a comment.

Requirements:
1. A brick library of at least 15 generic interlocking pieces (1x1 to 2x8 bricks, plates, slopes, round bricks, transparent windscreens and canopies) with accurate stud proportions on a stud grid. Each stud carries a small embossed original mark, not any real brand.
2. Building: pick a piece, rotate with keys, snap onto studs with a ghost preview showing valid or invalid placement, choose opaque or translucent colours, undo and redo, delete, copy a selection, and build on a baseplate.
3. Plastic materials: glossy ABS with a clearcoat, micro-surface imperfections from procedural roughness and normal maps (fine scratches, dust specks, faint fingerprints visible close up), and a subsurface-scattering approximation so light glows through brick edges, strongest in red, yellow and white.
4. Translucent pieces refract the scene behind them (screen-space refraction) and cast tinted light onto solid bricks below.
5. Stress test: in physics mode the model becomes rigid bodies joined by clutch joints of limited strength. Drop it, shake it on a quake table or hit it with a ball: overloaded connections show small gaps before they fail, and the model breaks into individual bricks that scatter and bounce.
6. Stress visualisation: clutch joints coloured by load before they break.
7. Stop-motion: a timeline of frames, each a snapshot of brick positions plus a few posable figures of your own original design, with onion-skinning of the previous frame, playback at 6, 12 or 24 fps, and a camera keyframed per frame.
8. Cinematic playback: depth of field, soft shadows, an adjustable three-point light rig, and optional film grain and vignette.
9. Export: record the animation to WebM with MediaRecorder from the canvas, save and load the model and timeline as JSON, and autosave to localStorage.
10. Instancing: bricks and studs drawn with InstancedMesh, so a 2,000-brick model stays smooth.
11. Camera: orbit, pan and zoom, top, front and side presets, and a macro close-up that shows the surface detail.
12. A settings panel exposes clutch strength, gravity, roughness and scratch intensity, subsurface strength and shadow quality, with reset to defaults.

Output one self-contained HTML file with inline JavaScript. Load Three.js (and any physics library you choose) from a CDN; build every model, texture and sound procedurally, with no external asset files. Use InstancedMesh for anything repeated, reuse geometries and materials, and stay smooth at 60 fps on a desktop GPU.
prompts.notes: Watch for: any real brand name or logo; missing or wrongly proportioned studs; bricks that do not snap; physics mode where the model falls as one rigid piece or explodes at the start; no visible imperfections or edge glow up close; stop-motion without onion skin or export.
